name: Konza Prairie and the Flint Hills
blurb: Bluestem, bison and spring fire in the last great tallgrass prairie.

tip.title: Take away fire
tip.text: Fire stops trees taking over. Set Fire to -100% and watch the grasses, then the bison, grasshoppers and prairie chickens that rely on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: The dominant tall grass of the Flint Hills prairie, and the main forage for grazing bison and cattle.
A tall warm-season grass that grows alongside big bluestem and is grazed by bison.
A shorter bunchgrass found on the thin, rocky upland soils of the Flint Hills.
A woody tree that spreads into unburned prairie; the Flint Hills are threatened by this woody encroachment.
A herd of about 200 bison grazes part of Konza Prairie. Wikipedia notes bison once grazed the region in huge numbers before being nearly wiped out.
Often present in large numbers at Konza. It browses wildflowers and shrubs, and its droppings add nutrients to the soil.
A common small grazer of grasses and wildflowers, and prey for many of the prairie predators.
A small grass-eating rodent that is well recorded around the park and is a staple prey of hawks and coyotes.
Eats seeds and fruit, plus insects such as grasshoppers in summer. The Flint Hills are known for it, and raccoons and other mesopredators take many eggs.
A grassland songbird recorded often near the park that eats insects and seeds.
An omnivore. Wikipedia notes mesopredators such as raccoons raise prairie-chicken egg losses.
A constrictor that eats rodents, rabbits and birds; GloBI records it feeding on rabbits and cotton rats.
A common raptor hunting voles, rabbits and ground birds over open prairie.
Scavenges carcasses such as deer and rabbits, returning their energy to the web.
The prairie's main wide-ranging carnivore, eating rabbits, rodents, insects and fawns.
A solitary cat that preys on rabbits, rodents and young deer.
Warm-season grasses grow fastest in summer sun.
Konza receives roughly 835 mm of rain a year, enough to support woodland if fire and grazing did not hold it back.
Fire keeps trees off the prairie and recycles nutrients; Flint Hills ranchers burn each spring to renew the grass.
Break down dead grass, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
